nameStory: The mink frog gets its unusual name from its distinctive smell, which supposedly resembles the musky scent of a mink. However, most people describe the odor as more like rotting onions than anything luxurious! This pungent aroma is released when the frog feels threatened, making it one of the few amphibians you can identify by nose alone.
description: The mink frog is a small to medium-sized water frog that spends most of its time in and around ponds and lakes. These hardy northerners have smooth, slippery skin that's typically olive-green to brown with darker spots or mottling across their back and legs. They're compact frogs, fitting comfortably in your cupped hands, with prominent eyes that help them spot prey both above and below the water's surface. Unlike some of their flashier cousins, mink frogs prefer to stay close to deeper water rather than venture far onto land.

idTips.label: Skin
idTips.description: Smooth, very slippery skin that feels almost slimy to the touch, with a distinctive musky smell like rotting onions when handled

idTips.label: Color/Pattern
idTips.description: Olive-green to brown back with darker irregular spots or blotches; belly is cream to pale yellow

idTips.label: Call
idTips.description: Deep, rapid tapping sound like wooden blocks being knocked together - 'tuk-tuk-tuk-tuk' - often heard at night

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found in or very close to permanent water bodies with lily pads and aquatic vegetation

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, prominent eyes with golden irises that seem oversized for their head

habitat: Mink frogs are found in permanent ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams, especially those with abundant aquatic vegetation like water lilies, cattails, and pondweeds. In New England, they prefer cooler northern waters and are most common in Vermont, New Hampshire, and northern Massachusetts. They rarely stray far from the water's edge, often sitting on lily pads or floating logs where they can quickly dive to safety.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots under logs or in mud at the bottom of ponds. Males begin calling from the water in late spring when temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding and calling season. Adults are most active at night, and you'll often hear their distinctive tapping calls from shoreline vegetation.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases as temperatures drop. Frogs begin moving to deeper water areas where they'll spend the winter.
seasonality.winter: Hibernate underwater in the mud at the bottom of ponds and lakes, or under submerged logs and debris.

funFact: Mink frogs can actually breathe underwater through their skin during winter hibernation, absorbing dissolved oxygen directly from the water around them while buried in pond mud for months at a time.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with green frogs, but mink frogs have that telltale oniony smell and prefer to stay right at the water's edge rather than hopping around on land. Remember: if it stinks like old onions and won't leave the lily pads, it's probably a mink frog!
contextualKnowledge: Also called the 'north frog' in some areas, reflecting their preference for cooler northern climates. The mink comparison in their name comes from the animal's musky scent glands, though most people find the frog's smell much less pleasant than actual mink musk.
compareHints: Unlike green frogs which have distinct ridges running down their backs and venture onto land regularly, mink frogs have smoother backs and stick close to water. They're smaller than bullfrogs and lack the leopard frog's crisp spotted pattern. The distinctive onion-like smell when handled sets them apart from all their water frog relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its water frog relatives, green frogs are larger than wood frogs and leopard frogs but smaller than bullfrogs, and they're the only ones that consistently show green coloring on the head.
Unlike the green frog which has prominent ridges down its back and lives near permanent water, wood frogs are smooth-backed forest dwellers.
Bullfrogs are significantly larger than their closest New England relatives like Green Frogs and Wood Frogs, and completely lack the fold-like ridges that run down the backs of Green Frogs.
Unlike the green frog which has prominent ridges running down its back, the pickerel frog's back is smooth between its square spots.
Unlike green frogs which have prominent ridges running down their backs, northern leopard frogs have smooth backs with only faint ridges.
Among its leopard frog relatives, the Atlantic Coast leopard frog is most similar to the Northern leopard frog but has a more restricted coastal range.
